courses.description: Would you like to take a class that is not offered at MVU? In this course, students will identify a topic of personal interest and/or or one relevant to their Pathway. Students will follow an organized but flexible executive function curriculum that allows them to build from whatever point they are starting from. Students will set clear learning goals, plan independent learning activities, monitor and track their progress, and design their own assessments with teacher support.

Students may earn elective credit by assisting teachers with classroom responsibilities, course preparation activities and/or tutoring fellow students. Students are required to attend an orientation and training at the beginning of each semester that will outline expectations for proficiency, which includes regular attendance. Teacher support will be assigned to one teacher, or a team/department. Peer tutors will be assigned to a department or class.

courses.course_name: ENGLISH 9: INTRODUCTION TO LITERATURE AND WRITING
courses.description: This course prepares students for success in high school level reading, writing, speaking, listening, and work habits. The course's essential question is “Who am I?”; students will explore who they are and who they want to become. The following skills are the prioritized learning for 9th grade students: citing textual evidence to support an analysis of a text, integrating useful evidence from credible sources, engaging thoughtfully in conversation about diverse topics and perspectives, and producing clear writing appropriate to task, purpose and audience. Instruction is differentiated by student learning style and ability, as well as student interest.
courses.notes: Honors credential in English 9 or 10 is referenced as an AP Language prerequisite

courses.description: This course supports students to make progress on ELA graduation proficiencies. The following skills are prioritized: reading for theme; analysis of informational text; collaborating in small and large group discussions about theme; research; the writing process including revision; and independent reading and writing. Instruction is differentiated by student learning style and ability, as well as student interest.
courses.prerequisites: English 9
courses.notes: Honors credential in English 9 or 10 is referenced as an AP Language prerequisite

courses.description: This course begins with an investigation of how students' choices affect themselves, others, and the world around them. Building on the ideas of their peers, students will clarify and challenge various points of view using evidence and reasoning. Students develop and refine the skills necessary for expository and argumentative writing for real-world audiences. Research methods and independent reading are integrated into the course.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of sophomore English

courses.description: This semester-long course is designed for first semester seniors to improve the language and writing skills of college bound students. The primary focus of this course is to examine strategies for writing effective scholarship and college admissions essays. Students will also study the SAT with a particular emphasis on vocabulary, timed-writing, and reading comprehension. We will prepare seniors for the SAT offered at MVU in the fall.
courses.prerequisites: Desire to attend college after high school
courses.fulfills_text: To fulfill the state and MVU requirements for graduation, a student must take two additional semesters of ELA electives beyond the 9-11th grade core classes.

courses.description: Students can fulfill either English or Social Studies graduation credit requirements by completing a community action research project. With support from English and Social Studies teachers, students will identify a compelling topic or local problem that stems from personal interests or career goals. Students will form questions to guide their research, locate a variety of reliable sources, organize their information and learning, and use their learning to better the community in some way. Students will discuss, support, and collaborate with peers, teachers, and community members. At the end of the course, students will share and celebrate their results. Credit may be applied to either ELA or Social Studies.
courses.fulfills_text: Students can fulfill either English or Social Studies graduation credit requirements
courses.notes: Also listed under Social Studies as 0220 HUMANITIES IN ACTION (same course; Social Studies listing adds that the project must have a heavy history focus to fulfill the history requirement)

courses.description: In this semester-long course, students will examine different monsters across various texts (literature, graphic novels, film, art) in order to answer the question, “How do monsters reflect the fears of a society?” Students will explore who and what a society determines to be a monster and, in turn, what this says about the culture that created it. Students will close-read written and visual texts to discover who or what the monster is and evaluate why it exists. Students will write a variety of creative and essay assignments to deepen their understanding of genre, specific readings, and common themes found in literature with monstrous characters.
courses.fulfills_text: To fulfill the state and MVU requirements for graduation, a student must take two additional semesters of ELA electives beyond the 9-11th grade core classes.

courses.description: This course is designed to assist students in developing practical skills for effective public speaking. Students will select and organize ideas, support ideas clearly and logically, adapt performances and messages to particular audiences with a close study of rhetoric, and deliver effective messages with confidence and enthusiasm. Students will develop and refine lifelong skills essential to the workplace and to becoming a more engaged citizen in society. Students will be immersed in various forms of spoken expression including impromptu speeches, informational presentations, persuasive performances, and oral storytelling.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of English 10
courses.fulfills_text: To fulfill the state and MVU requirements for graduation, a student must take two additional semesters of ELA electives beyond the 9-11th grade core classes.

courses.description: This course is designed for students who plan to pursue a job-oriented path after high school. Students will develop reading and writing skills that will be required in technical careers such as those in the trades or office professions. Students will learn how to read informational texts like technical manuals, computer programs, and blueprints. Students will master content-specific vocabulary and practice crafting formal correspondence and technical instructive writing (i.e. manuals). The reading and writing skills developed in this course will support students’ transition from high school to a professional career.
courses.fulfills_text: To fulfill the state and MVU requirements for graduation, a student must take two additional semesters of ELA electives beyond the 9-11th grade core classes.

courses.description: recommendation, strong English skills, and self-motivation (summer assignment required). Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines This course is designed to take your awareness of both the reading and writing processes to the highest level in preparation for college. In reading, the mastery of rhetorical analysis is a key goal, as is more self awareness of reading strategies such as making inferences, recognizing tone, and distinguishing shades of meaning. In writing, we will do intensive work at organizing more complex expository structures, developing new levels of fluency in structure and diction, and more full development of evidence. Students enrolled in this course will be prepared to take the Advanced Placement examination, but taking the official exam in May is not required.
courses.prerequisites: successful completion of an honors credential in English 9 or 10, teacher/counselor
courses.notes: Section prerequisite: Capability to do college level work and teacher/counselor approval

courses.description: Placement Literature elective must meet certain criteria for enrollment. Students must read at grade level, and complete a summer reading and writing assignment. Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines This course is designed to prepare students to reason and write at a level expected of moderately to highly competitive colleges. AP Literature introduces students to the language of literary analysis. Students may be required to read as many as twenty pages per night to complete the chosen major works of world literature which make the core foundation of this course. Through reading, writing, and Socratic discussion, students evaluate adult literary themes and concepts in order to develop a sensitivity to, and appreciation of, the literary work, its language, character, theme, structure, and meaning. Most written pieces will be timed (on-demand), but students are also expected to process pieces. Students enrolled in this course will be prepared to take the Advanced Placement examination, but taking the official exam in May is not required. In preparation for this course, students are required to complete summer reading and writing projects which are factored into the first quarter grade average.
courses.prerequisites: Due to the challenging expectations of this course, students choosing to take the Advanced
courses.notes: Section prerequisite: Capability to do college level work and teacher/counselor approval

courses.description: This course is designed to help students develop an appreciation and understanding of cultures, religions, people, and events through history and make connections to their present day lives. The first half of the year is focused on developing an understanding of cultures from around the world, while learning how to construct an argument using claim, evidence and reasoning. In the second half of the year students are developing inquiry projects and forming solutions to global problems. Students will have an opportunity throughout the year to make choices about how they show their understanding of the key skills while at the same time focusing on issues and topics of interest.
courses.notes: Students are encouraged to opt to complete the honors credential in 9th and 10th grade social studies

courses.description: This standards-based college preparatory course will provide students with an understanding of the important trends in the history of our nation and state. Focus is on citizens’ rights, change over time, inquiry, and key events such as the Civil War, Westward Expansion, Industrialization, the Great Depression, and the World Wars. Emphasis is on the skills of writing, discussion, and making connections over history.
courses.notes: Students are encouraged to opt to complete the honors credential in 9th and 10th grade social studies

courses.description: This course is a capstone to a student's social studies experience at MVU, designed to bring together the previous five years of learning to ensure they are prepared for adult life. Students must demonstrate their ability to be an informed and engaged citizen, to manage a budget and navigate a ballot, and to be part of a successful family, town, state, and nation. Field Trips, discussions, class simulations and games, independent research, and community projects will help students gain the knowledge and understanding needed. Class materials will include Town Reports, federal budgets, Town Meeting ballots, zoning by-laws, Vermont Bar Association's Your Legal Rights @ Eighteen, and various other government and legal documents. 10 hours of community service will be completed during the course within class-designed projects and field trips. Since much of the course requirements are in-person and hands-on, timeliness, attendance and participation are essential to receiving credit. *This course is required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is required for graduation.

courses.description: The Green Mountain State has a unique and storied history. In this class students will learn about Vermont's links to events that are covered in Social Studies classes all over the country. The Revolutionary War? It happened here. The Civil War? Vermonters were key combatants in that conflict. The Prohibition Era? It unfolded right here in Vermont. Rail History? There were railroads in Vermont before they were out west! In this course, students will learn about Vermonters who changed the course of history.

This course is designed to expose students to the enormous amount of local history that exists in Franklin County and Vermont. Students will learn how large national events unfolded here at home, and conduct group and individual inquiry projects using local resources such as historical societies, archeological digs, and historians or experts. Students will be expected to participate in numerous class discussions and hands-on learning opportunities. Some work will also be done using Ancestry.com and online sources to trace local family lines. The class will also explore the Abenaki/NativAmerican history of the region.

This course is an exploration of the role of war throughout history. Students will research topics of personal interest related to war, and discuss current conflicts in the world. Students will complete small scale inquiries, as well as an in-depth historian project. Movies, music and other media will be used to show the impacts of war on soldiers, veterans and their families, civilians, leaders, and the environment.

This course is designed to examine historical and contemporary subjects through modern film, music, and art. The media will investigate how society changes or informs our perceptions of ourselves and our society. This is a discussion-based class with the opportunity to learn how to develop, articulate, and argue opinions and positions. Students will examine politics, climate, urban development, food, war, government, art, animal rights, and contemporary issues related to high school students and their interests.

This course is designed for those who are interested in college level work, but need more support in time management, organization, test and note taking skills. The first semester will focus on those college skills and will gradually build in the content of U.S. government and politics. The second semester will focus on both the study of general concepts of U.S. government and politics, and the analysis of specific examples of current events, policy, media, and court cases, including those from local and Vermont government.Topics covered will be: The Constitution, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties, Interest Groups, Mass Media, Institutions of National Government, Public Policy, and Civil Rights and Liberties. *Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.
courses.notes: Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV

courses.description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. Advanced Placement Psychology focuses on the evolution of modern psychology, different approaches to psychology, and advanced topics like abnormal psychology. The course follows the rigorous AP curriculum established by the College Board, including in-depth study of a variety of concepts, issues, and theories in the field of Psychology. Students will use a scientific approach to investigate human behavior and mental processes. Specific topics of study include memory, sensation and perception, personality, psychological disorders and treatments, and social psychology. The culminating activity of the course will be the AP examination by which students may earn college credit for their work. Students who are considering careers in social services or in psychology are encouraged to take this class. *Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.
courses.notes: Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV

courses.description: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2026-27 Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. AP United States Government and Politics is a year-long course that will give students an analytical perspective on government and politics in the United States. This course includes both the study of general concepts of U.S. government and politics, and the analysis of specific examples of current events, policy, media, and court cases, including those from local and Vermont governments. In the preparation of the AP exam, topics covered will be: Constitutional Underpinnings of United States Government, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties, Interest Groups, and Mass Media, Institutions of National Government, Public Policy, and Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, Community Service is a requirement for this class as well.
courses.offering_note: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2026-27

courses.description: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2027-2028 Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons, and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society. The course follows the rigorous AP curriculum established by the College Board. The culminating activity of the course will be the AP examination by which students may earn college credit for their work. Sophomores must get a teacher's recommendation.
courses.offering_note: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2027-2028 (not offered 2026-27)

courses.description: This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability, geometry, and discrete mathematics. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum.

Geometry topics include constructions, circle properties, similarity, algebraic reasoning, trigonometric ratios, properties of quadrilaterals and triangles, proofs of theorems, transformations. Course instruction includes investigations that are designed to help students apply geometry concepts as they explore problems and make connections with other areas of mathematics.

Algebra II is a continuation of Algebra I. Advanced Algebraic reasoning is emphasized in this course. Topics include solving equations and inequalities, solving polynomial and rational functions, as well as a catalog of elementary functions including but not limited to linear functions, absolute value functions, piecewise functions and square root functions.

This course is designed for students who wish to take AP Calculus or AP Statistics by their senior year. Algebra II will be held daily for Semester 1 and Pre-Calculus will be held daily for Semester 2. Algebra II requirements must be met by the end of semester one in order to continue to Pre-calculus semester 2. Upon completion of Pre-Calculus you will receive 2 credits. A math teacher must recommend a student.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course is designed for those students who are planning to take calculus or other advanced math courses. Topics covered include linear and nonlinear functions, analytic geometry, trigonometry, logarithms, complex numbers, and sequences and series. * Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.
courses.prerequisites: Passing completion of Algebra II or Math in Action Recommendation
courses.notes: Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV

courses.description: This course builds on the foundations of Algebra 1 and Geometry through a project-based approach that emphasizes real-world applications, collaboration, and problem-solving. Students will explore key practical math concepts—including geometric construction, scale drawings, systems of inequalities, and exponential growth—by engaging in hands-on projects that connect mathematics to authentic contexts.
courses.prerequisites: Passing Completion of Algebra and Geometry

courses.description: This course covers the basics of statistics and data analysis. Students will learn how to collect, organize, and interpret data using graphs, charts, averages, and simple probability. Emphasis is placed on real-world examples and developing a practical understanding of how data is used in everyday life. No advanced math skills are required beyond basic algebra.

Explore how trigonometry is used in the real world to solve practical problems in science, engineering, architecture, navigation, and design. Focusing on topics that show up in various careers, such as Construction, Electrical work, Architecture, Surveying, Engineering, and more. Learn about angles, right triangles, Laws of Sines and Cosines, and trigonometric functions through real-life applications like measuring distances, modeling waves, and interpreting data. This course emphasizes problem-solving, critical thinking, and the use of technology to connect math to everyday life.
courses.prerequisites: Passing Completion of Algebra and Geometry

courses.description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines This is a rigorous full year course in Calculus AP as prescribed by the College Board that incorporates two broadly based conceptual themes. The two themes are differential calculus and integral calculus with applications. A student in this class must be prepared to complete independent work daily outside of class time. A student in this class must be prepared to spend 1 ½ to 2 hours of study time for each hour of class time. This course requires the use of the TI-84 plus graphing calculator for technology support.
courses.prerequisites: Passing completion of Pre-Calculus

courses.description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines This is a rigorous full year course in Statistics as prescribed by the College Board that incorporates three broadly based conceptual themes. The three themes are descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and experiment design. A student in this class must be prepared to spend a minimum of 1 ½ to 2 hrs of study time for each hour of class time. This course requires the use of the TI-84 plus graphing calculator for technology support.
courses.prerequisites: Passing completion of Algebra II or Math in Action Teacher Recommendation

courses.description: All freshman students are required to take a sequence of science literacy courses as recommended by the Next Generation Science Standards. The units of study are forces and motion, electromagnetic radiation, waves, energy, properties of matter, and chemical reactions. Students will learn content through the application of the science and engineering practices and cross cutting concepts.
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to take a three year sequence of science literacy courses

courses.description: All sophomore students are required to take this science literacy course as recommended by the Next Generation Science Standards . There is also a one semester elective companion course labeled CP Biology that offers some traditional topics that supplement the Science 10 course available to the sophomore class. Along with the Science and Engineering standards and the Cross-Cutting Concepts outlined in the NGSS, the following units address a variety of Disciplinary Core Ideas: Interdependent Relationships in Ecosystems Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms The Universe and Its Stars Growth and Development of Organisms Structure and Function Variation of Traits
courses.fulfills_text: All students are required to take a three year sequence of science literacy courses

courses.description: This course is designed for students interested in learning about science in our everyday lives without the focus on college preparatory skills of the other science electives. In this course, students will discover how chemical reactions create the foods we eat and how the properties of molecules change our ingredients. Students will answer questions such as why is butter solid at room temperature and vegetable oil liquid? What does tenderizing meat do? Why does bread rise? Why don’t some ingredients interact?

College Preparatory Earth and Space Science is a Fall or Spring Semester elective designed to supplement the Science 9 curriculum. There is an emphasis on developing skills that will enable students to be better prepared for the rigor of advanced courses such as CP Biology, CP Chemistry, CP Physics, and AP Biology. Topics include: astronomy (galaxies, solar system, current day explorations), atmosphere, and climate (global warming and ice ages). Students will be required to develop science literacy and computational (math) skills.

College Preparatory Biology is a Spring Semester elective designed to supplement the Science 10 curriculum with some of the traditional units of study for students who are truly interested in science and preparing for the advanced College Preparatory Electives that are offered in grades 11-12. Microbiology, plants and animals are topics to be discussed. Students will be required to write format lab reports, read primary literature, and to become active learners through activity-based explorations that promote further opportunity to apply the Science and Engineering practices.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of CP Earth and Space

courses.course_name: CP CHEMISTRY FALL - Liquids and Gases
courses.description: This elective is recommended for students intending to follow a science based course of study in college. Topics of study for this rigorous course includes a brief review of chemical bonding, an in depth exploration of chemical reactions and stoichiometry, solutions, solubility, and concentration. Content is delivered through a combination of hands-on exploratory activities, note taking, practice problems and mini-labs that challenge students to use their critical thinking and problem solving skills.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of CP Bio

courses.course_name: CP CHEMISTRY SPRING - Energy and Electrons
courses.description: This elective is a continuation of CP Chemistry Fall and is recommended for students intending to follow a science based course of study in college. Topics of study for this rigorous course include an in depth exploration of pH/acids/bases, gases and gas laws, thermochemistry, and oxidation/reduction. Similarly to CP Chemistry Fall, content is delivered through a combination of hands-on exploratory activities, note taking, practice problems and mini-labs that challenge students to use their critical thinking and problem solving skills.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of CP Bio and CP Chemistry Fall

courses.description: A survey of human anatomy and physiology. Topics will include the organization and structure of the major body systems and will include topics such as body tissues, muscular system, immune system, cancer, circulatory system, nervous system, and respiratory system. Emphasis placed on how the structure of our different body systems allows them to function properly in the human body

This course for juniors and seniors covers the basic concepts of a typical first semester introductory physics course for college students. Topics include: linear and 2-dimensional kinematics, vectors, forces, simple harmonic motion and mechanical energy. Concepts are explored through formal and informal laboratory investigations with formal lab reports. Physics Olympics events, and quantitative problem solving using algebra, trigonometry and graphical analysis techniques are also emphasized. This one semester elective in physics is not required as a prerequisite for Physics - Electromagnetism and Waves in Spring semester and vice versa. Due to the frequent use of mathematics in Physics, it is strongly recommended that students have completed Algebra 2 and are enrolled in Advanced Math.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Science 10 and strong Math skills
courses.notes: Scheduled as 1 Period; College Prep (CP) science course

courses.description: This course for juniors and seniors covers the basic concepts of a typical second semester introductory physics course for college students. Topics include: optics, wave mechanics, sound, electricity, magnetism, and electric circuits. Concepts are explored through formal and informal laboratory investigations with formal lab reports, as well as quantitative problem solving using algebra, trigonometry and graphical analysis techniques. The final project includes designing, wiring, building and testing a loudspeaker system. This one semester elective in physics does not require Physics - Newtonian Mechanics in the fall semester and vice versa. Due to the frequent use of mathematics in Physics, it is strongly recommended that students have completed Algebra 2 and are enrolled in Advanced Math.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Science 10 and strong Math skills

courses.description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines AP biology is designed to help prepare students for the Advanced Placement Biology exam during the second week in May. Complex concepts are explored through a set of required, open-minded research investigations. The exploration and discovery of science and mathematics goes beyond data collecting and focuses on data analysis in conjunction with theoretical modeling. Biotechnology topics include: electrophoresis, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of DNA and bacterial DNA transformation. Summer coursework is required. The Big Ideas of AP Biology: Big Idea 1: The process of evolution drives the diversity and unity of life. Big Idea 2: Biological systems utilize free energy and molecular building blocks to grow, to reproduce, and to maintain dynamic homeostasis. Big Idea 3: Living systems store, retrieve, transmit, and respond to information essential to life processes. Big Idea 4: Biological systems interact, and these systems and their interactions possess complex properties.
courses.prerequisites: CP Chemistry Fall-Liquids & Gases and CP Chemistry Spring-Energy & Electrons

courses.description: This semester course provides students with hands-on experience in a variety of the techniques used by forensic investigators. It is designed to focus on four major units of study: body decomposition, blood spatter analysis, fingerprint analysis and identification, and finally, forensic anthropology. Concepts related to each unit of study are explored through a variety of activities including a month-long investigation centered around altering the rate of decomposition, qualitative and quantitative analysis of blood spatter stains, ridgeline pattern identification and matching for unknown prints, and finally, examining distinctive bone features in order to identify an unknown skeleton. Due to the frequent use of mathematics in each unit, it is strongly recommended that students have completed Algebra 2.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Science 10

courses.description: This course examines the relationships between living things and their environment and how humans affect them in both positive and negative ways. We will discuss current events and environmental topics and not shy away from examining controversial issues. Field work activities are integrated to allow students to apply the techniques professional wildlife biologists use. Some examples of field work include using the capture-mark-recapture method to estimate the population of fish in a nearby stream, and using trail cameras to survey predator diversity in the woods near school.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of two science courses

courses.description: This pre-technical exploratory course introduces students to all aspects of Diversified Agriculture, including but not limited to Sustainable Agriculture Systems, Agricultural Mechanical Systems, Agricultural Safety, Greenhouse/Horticulture Management and Soils, and Agribusiness .Classroom instruction is supplemented with a wide variety of hands-on, experiential learning in the livestock barn, the green house, the land lab, the wood shop, and the mechanic shop. Students who successfully complete this course are encouraged to enroll in Sustainable Agriculture or Agricultural Mechanics I.

This technical course introduces students to applied mechanics in agricultural settings. It covers essential skills such as basic woodworking, electrical systems, plumbing, concrete work, land measurement, small engines, and equipment maintenance (including oil changes, greasing, cleaning, fluid level checks, and air filter replacements). Students will be trained and continuously evaluated on workplace safety practices. Additionally, students will receive training and certification in CPR/AED and basic first aid. They will learn the fundamentals of two-stroke and four-stroke gasoline engines, as well as how to use measurement tools like micrometers, calipers, depth gauges, and other intricate measuring instruments. The course also includes instruction in welding (both Arc and Gas), CNC plasma cutting, and metal fabrication. Field trips, guest speakers, and representatives from technical schools will provide students with insights into educational and career opportunities in the mechanics field, both locally and nationally. The primary emphasis at this level is on safety, skill development, career awareness, personal responsibility, teamwork, and professionalism. Students who successfully complete this class will earn an Industry-Recognized Credential (IRC) in EETC small engine mechanics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Intro to Diversified Ag or instructor’s permission

courses.description: This technical education course builds on the foundational knowledge and skills acquired in Ag Mechanics I. Students will deepen their understanding through continued instruction, practice, and increasingly complex projects. They will be trained and continuously evaluated on workplace safety, personal responsibility, teamwork, and professionalism. Students will earn certifications in advanced CPR/AED and Stop the Bleed. The focus will be on applying their fundamental skills to intermediate and advanced projects, including on-campus agriculture and athletic building construction, as well as equipment and agricultural implement repair. In this course, students will learn MIG welding and advance their skills in stick and gas welding, alongside various fabrication projects. They will also gain knowledge in irrigation installation and repair, concrete installation and repair, and other projects designed to enhance their skills and abilities. Students will learn how to estimate material costs, determine the number of hours required, and identify the tools needed for various projects. Additionally, they will learn appropriate record-keeping systems to accurately manage these projects. Field trips, guest speakers, and representatives from technical schools will provide students with insights into educational and career paths in the mechanics field, both locally and nationally. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be well-prepared for a Cooperative Training Experience in their senior year of high school. They will also earn one (1) science credit and an Industry-Recognized Credential (IRC) in Stick and MIG welding.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Ag Mechanics I or instructor’s permission

courses.description: Students enrolled in Sustainable Agriculture will explore the foundations of modern, environmentally responsible agricultural practices. This course emphasizes the connections between science, technology, and business in the production and processing of food, fiber, and other agricultural products. Students will investigate where and how food is produced, analyze current agricultural trends, and evaluate their impact on the future of food systems and natural resources.Through classroom instruction, laboratory experiences, and hands-on learning, students will develop skills in sustainable farming practices, animal husbandry, and agribusiness management. Topics include defining sustainable agriculture, employee and animal safety, CPR certification, animal handling, animal health and well-being, anatomy and physiology, animal nutrition, and reproduction. Students will also engage in food processing, entrepreneurship, business design and finance, sales and marketing, and record keeping.All students will participate in an SAE (Supervised Agricultural Experience) project and develop leadership skills through FFA participation and career-based learning opportunities.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Intro to Diversified Ag or instructor endorsement.

courses.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive introduction to veterinary science through the Cornell Veterinary Science Curriculum for High School Students. Topics include the care and management of both small and large animals, biosecurity practices within veterinary settings, veterinary terminology, and an in-depth study of animal anatomy and physiology. Students will develop a foundational understanding of the animal industry and progress toward exploring the structure and function of different body systems across species. This course also incorporates leadership and experiential learning through participation in the Missisquoi Valley Union (MVU) FFA Chapter and the completion of a Supervised Agricultural Experience (SAE) project.
courses.prerequisites: STUDENTS MUST BE 16 YEARS OLD

courses.course_name: AG & NATURAL RESOURCES Cooperative Technical Education
courses.description: Cooperative Technical Education (CTE) is a career training experience in which students are placed in paid work experiences at training stations directly related to their technical education program. A training plan and a WBL agreement are required, and must be completed and approved prior to enrollment in this program. Characteristics, duration and credits are determined in the training plan. See the MVUHS Work-Based Learning Coordinator for more information.
courses.credits_text: Credits and Duration determined on individual student and placement
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of a Level I and II course of study with Instructors endorsement.

courses.description: Students will practice expressing themselves in Spanish in practical, real-life situations. They will develop their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills through functional and proficiency - based activities. Students will learn to understand and manipulate the structures of the language necessary for basic communication. They will receive an overview of Hispanic culture and customs. This course partially fulfills the second language requirements of many colleges.

Students will continue to develop the listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills begun in Spanish I. They will become more proficient in spontaneous use of the language and will continue to make real-life and functional applications. The students will study the culture of Spain and Latin America and will understand the role of Hispanic customs and peoples in the United States. This course partially fulfills the second language requirements of many colleges.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish I or 7th & 8th grade Spanish

courses.description: This course will continue to develop the listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills of the previous level. Students will become more proficient in the language and more familiar with the Hispanic culture and civilization of Spain, Latin America, and the United States. Students will learn the career applications of second language study and will further develop the functional skills necessary to use the language for work, travel, and personal goals.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish II

courses.description: In this course students will survey the literature, history, and contemporary culture of the Hispanic world. A comprehensive review of the structure of the language may be used to prepare those students who wish to meet college admission requirements. A variety of technology and media in the target language will be used.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish III

courses.description: Students will practice expressing themselves in French in practical, real-life situations. They will develop their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills through functional and proficiency based activities. Students will learn to understand and manipulate the structures of the language necessary for basic communication. They will receive an overview of French culture and customs including the United States, Canada, and the French-speaking world. This course partially fulfills the second language requirements of many colleges.

Students will continue to develop the listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills begun in French I. They will become more proficient in spontaneous use of the language and will continue to make real-life and functional applications. The students will study the culture of France, Canada, and the French-speaking world. Students will understand the role of Francophone cultures and customs in the United States. This course partially fulfills the second language requirements of many colleges.
courses.prerequisites: French I or 7th & 8th grade French

courses.description: This course will continue to develop the listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills of the previous level. Students will become more proficient in the use of the language and more familiar with the French culture of France, Canada, and other areas of the French-speaking world. Students will learn the career applications of second language study and will further develop the functional skills necessary to use the language for work, travel, and personal goals.
courses.prerequisites: French II

courses.description: In this course students will survey the literature, history, and contemporary culture of the French-speaking world. A comprehensive review of the structure of the language may be used to prepare those students who wish to meet college admission requirements. A variety of technology and media in the target language will be used. BUSINESS EDUCATION All people apply business concepts and skills throughout their lives. To prepare students for their roles as citizens, consumers, and workers, the business curriculum presents learning opportunities for (a) understanding fundamental economic and business concepts; (b) developing positive dispositions for working and living in a changing environment; (c) making wise economic and career choices; and (d) securing knowledge and skills necessary for success on the job.
courses.prerequisites: French III

courses.description: In this course, students learn about the basic fundamentals of business. Areas of study will include owning and operating a business, management, accounting, marketing, and advertising. This course provides an overview of the most current business practices, knowledge, and skills needed by every worker.

Explore the intriguing world of sports and entertainment from the perspective of marketing. This course will take you on a step-by step journey through the exciting world of sports and entertainment marketing. You will learn about the key functions of marketing and how those functions are applied to the sports, recreation and entertainment industries. Guest speakers, case studies, projects, online activities of owning your own professional sports team will broaden the classroom learning experience.

This course will focus on the basic principles of sound personal financial management. Students will learn about financial goals and decision making, cash flow and budgeting, banking skills, auto and renters’ insurance, and use/misuse of credit. *Required for graduation
courses.prerequisites: Career Exploration

courses.description: This class is a place to explore career clusters and specific careers through many resources. It provides time to start planning for life after high school and to develop productive goals, which could include postsecondary education/training, internship or apprenticeship programs, military branch positions, and/or employment opportunities. *Required for graduation

This course is for students interested in immediate skills for entry or advancement in the job market. Also, students planning on majoring in Accounting or Business in college, should take this course. Topics covered include journals, ledgers, worksheets, financial statements, and payroll with an emphasis on the “how” of recording and posting transactions.

Driver education is using differentiated instruction to integrate other subject areas into the curriculum, while meeting the needs of students at their individual readiness level, to increase the understanding of all students. Individual students will utilize different methods to explore the same key concepts of habit development for risk management. Students develop strategies to manage the risks associated with sharing the road with other roadway users. Students are assessed based on their attitude, behaviors, and skills. Students are graded based on their ability to recall information provided and discovered through coverage of the Vermont Driver Education Curriculum. Attendance, participation, and practice are crucial to the successful completion of this course. Students learn to strive toward balance for their mind, body, and vehicle. Behind the wheel instruction is provided concurrently with the classroom lessons, allowing students to visualize and practice classroom concepts. It is highly recommended that students taking Driver Education have a study hall to fulfill the driving requirement. Students will drive during study halls or elective classes. Limited “after school” driving may be available. To comply with the state requirements and the state’s new GDL (Graduated Driver’s License) law, students must have access to driving practice time at home, and have their learner’s permit for one year before obtaining a driver’s license. Students who accumulate more than 5 absences may be dropped from the course.
courses.prerequisites: Valid Vermont Learner’s Permit & Attend a “Parent/Guardian & Student Night”

courses.description: This required course is designed to aid students in their transition from adolescence to young adulthood. Students will learn behaviors and practice skills that will help them make informed, healthy choices that positively affect the health, safety, and well-being of themselves and others. A variety of teen issues are discussed that focus on decision making and problem solving skills. Specific units of study include: Mental Health and Wellness, Alcohol, Tobacco and Other Drugs, and Interpersonal Relationships.

This introductory course establishes the foundation for physical literacy. Students are exposed to a broad range of team, individual, and fitness activities, with an emphasis on basic skill acquisition, rules, etiquette, and the fundamental components of health-related fitness. The course introduces students to the four critical proficiencies and guides them through initial self-assessments and goal-setting activities.

Advanced PE builds upon the skills and concepts learned in PE 1, moving students toward independent application of knowledge and advanced strategy. Students will participate in a variety of individual and dual games, team games, and fitness-based activities with a focus on applying movement principles, improving performance, and understanding the long-term benefits of active living.
courses.prerequisites: Intro to PE or Counselor/teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course focuses on developing the skills and knowledge needed to pursue recreational and outdoor activities for enjoyment and sustained wellness. Units may include archery, golf, hiking, orienteering, snowshoeing, cross country skiing, disc golf, or fitness center protocols. Emphasis is placed on personal choice, planning, and evaluation of activities as a primary means of maintaining health outside of a school environment.
courses.prerequisites: PE 1 or teacher recommendation

courses.course_name: Independent Study / Flexible Pathway (By Application Only)
courses.description: Students will design a Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) with a supervising PE teacher. The plan must clearly define specific, measurable, advanced performance goals in one or more PBGR domains. Assessment requires a detailed portfolio of evidence (e.g., training logs, video journals, analysis papers, and a final presentation/demonstration) proving independent mastery of the selected PBGR indicators. Criteria for Enrollment: Limited to specific circumstances such as: (1) Students engaged in high-level athletic training that exceeds the scope of standard courses (e.g., competitive dance, specialized martial arts, elite sports); (2) Students with schedule conflicts that prevent course enrollment; or (3) Long term medical restrictions/exemptions
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of PE 1 & PE 2, and formal approval by a PE teacher and administration.

courses.description: Students who participate in interscholastic athletics at Missisquoi Valley UHS or another VPA member school may apply for credit towards graduation requirements in physical education 1. A student must participate in two (2) sports seasons to become eligible for this credit opportunity, and may earn no more than ½ credit for successful completion of these seasons. 2. A student must participate in the sports season for its entirety in order to receive credit. Receipt of a certificate from the Athletic Department will constitute successful completion of the sports season. Students who do not complete a season (leave or are suspended from the team, cut from the team, or become academically ineligible) may not use that sports season for credit. This will be documented by the Director of Athletics. 3. The use of this credit option must be completed before starting a student’s senior year of school. 4. The interscholastic athletics credit option for physical education will appear as a “P” on the student’s transcript, and will not be counted as part of a student’s grade point average (GPA). 5. This credit option in physical education must be approved by both the Guidance Department and the Administration. ** May only be added to your schedule by your guidance counselor**
courses.prerequisites: PE 1 & PE 2 and completion of 2 sport seasons
courses.notes: May earn no more than 1/2 credit for two sport seasons; appears as P on transcript

courses.description: This course, which introduces students to three-dimensional art. The 26-27 school year’s focus will be ceramics.The focus is on design skills, craftsmanship and the introduction of a variety of techniques. Students explore additive and subtractive sculptural techniques, designing in the round, and contemporary crafts and ceramics .Classwork includes hand building techniques. This hands-on course incorporates various materials, techniques, and art history while utilizing the Elements of Art and Principles of Design. Materials may include clay, cardboard, wire, plaster and mixed media. Students will participate in the three-dimensional art processes from design through completion. Students will continue to explore self-expression and creativity to solve design problems. This course can be taken repeatedly. Students who take 3D Studio 1 & 2 are eligible to take AP Art.

The 26-27 school year’s focus will be ceramics. This course is a continuation of the concepts and processes learned in 3D Studio i.e., advanced hand building and the creation of ceramic sculpture and functional forms as well as introducing more advanced skills. Students will expand their skills, techniques and understanding of three-dimensional concepts and materials. Students will further explore various decoration techniques and continue to develop their three-dimensional problem-solving skills and learn the history of ceramics. Projects are more thematically driven and independently developed from conception to completion. This course can be taken repeatedly. Students who take 3D Studio 1 & 2 are eligible to take AP Art.
courses.prerequisites: 3D Studio 1

courses.description: This is a foundation studio art course that concentrates on the Elements of Art and Design through drawing, painting, mixed media, and sculpture. Students learn by using a variety of media such as pencil, ink, charcoal, paint, and other materials. Art history and a variety of art making techniques are part of the course. A sketchbook will be used for in class assignments and practice work.

This course builds on the techniques and skills developed in Art 1. Students will be introduced to new drawing techniques, develop their drawing skills, methods, and use of different materials while working to develop creative problem-solving skills. Drawing from life enhances observational skills relating to value, scale, proportion, composition, value, etc. Projects may include studies of value, still-life, self-portraits and nature studies using a variety of materials such as charcoal, graphite, alcohol marker, conte and colored pencil. This course can be taken repeatedly. Students who take 2 semesters of this course, or pair it with Painting and are eligible to take AP Art.
courses.prerequisites: Art 1 or with Instructor approval

courses.description: This course builds on the techniques and skills developed in Art 1. Students will focus on various painting styles, composition, and color theory through the art-making process and will be introduced to new painting techniques, methods and materials while working to develop creative problem-solving skills. Students will use watercolor, gouache, acrylic, and oil paint. This course can be taken repeatedly. Students who take 2 semesters of this course, or pair it with Drawing and are eligible to take AP Art.
courses.prerequisites: Art 1 or with Instructor approval

courses.description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. This course is intended for highly motivated art students committed to the serious study of art, and art making. This portfolio prep course promotes critical thinking and the development of art technique, composition, and content/idea. Students will be given the freedom to work in the medium of their choice, but are also encouraged to explore, experiment, and develop their own identifiable style. This course includes intensive studio work, participation in school & community art shows, class and individual critiques, weekly homework assignments, and the expectation that AP Art students will work outside of class time on their portfolio. Students will submit an AP Art Portfolio to the College Board in the spring.
courses.prerequisites: 2 semesters of Drawing or Painting, Graphic Design 2, 3D Studio 2 OR with Instructor Approval

courses.description: The aim of this course is for students to become proficient in design principles and techniques. The course will focus on using and learning industry standard software, Adobe Photoshop and Procreate (iPad), creating digital artwork that reflects traditional graphic design methods. The students will work as individuals and collaboratively throughout the course.
courses.prerequisites: Art I

courses.description: This is an intermediate/advanced level course that expands the skills and knowledge mastered in Graphic Design I. The course emphasizes practical assignments that apply problem solving and professional solutions for graphic design. The course will focus on using and learning industry standard software, Adobe Illustrator, Students who pass this course are eligible to take AP Art.
courses.prerequisites: Graphic Design I

courses.description: Learn how to cook and bake many healthy meals and snacks! Students work in groups to create dishes that are inexpensive and healthy and are able to be recreated at home. Interspersed with the cooking labs, the students will have the opportunity to learn good nutrition principles that are necessary for physical and mental wellness and a long, healthy life. Instructional materials include discussions of digestion, basic nutrients, diet analysis, sports and fitness, and life-span nutrition.
courses.notes: Listed under Fine Arts; also a Family & Consumer Science (cooking) course

courses.description: Create and produce cooking shows,short food reels and creative food tutorials inspired by current social media trends and popular cooking content(British Bake Off, Food Wars, Master Chef, Is it cake?) Learning outcomes: Enhanced Media Literacy, video editing,ethical media use, creative writing, marketing and culinary presentation.

This choir is open to all high school students who wish to sing. We perform in concerts 4 times a year while working on technique, blend, and musicianship. Festival opportunities are open to all and are strongly encouraged.

An audition is required to become a member of this selected performance group of 10-16 singers. The ability to read music becomes more important as Master Singers perform at a more difficult level of music than Concert Choir. Singers in this small group need to blend, sing independently, have a strong sense of ensemble, and are clearly committed to performance. Repertoire will emphasize work from the Renaissance through contemporary music. Participation in District Music festival auditions is expected, along with performing at extra events such as Madrigal Festival and more. Formal concert attire is required.
courses.prerequisites: Must successfully complete Concert Choir for one year and pass an audition.

courses.description: This course is for somewhat advanced students who have participated in Middle School Band and have demonstrated advanced technical skills. Master musicianship, technique, and performance related music theory skills will be emphasized. Students will perform music commensurate with grade level II - III (on a music grading scale of I-VI). Some activities will occur outside of the regular class period. Marching Band and concerts are required of all students in the band program. Participation in District and All State Festivals will be encouraged.
courses.prerequisites: Previous Band experience

courses.description: Students in this course gain skill in playing advanced band literature and develop independence in reading and rhythmic skills. It requires a high degree of proficiency on an individual instrument. This course is for advanced students who have passed a rigorous audition and have demonstrated advanced technical skills. Master musicianship, technique and performance related music theory skills will be emphasized. Students will perform music commensurate with grade level II - III(on music grading scale of I-VI). Some activities will occur outside of the regular class period. Marching Band and concerts are required of all students in the band program. Participation in District and All State Festivals will be strongly encouraged. Students are selected from the Wind Ensemble for participation in Music Pit Band, Stage Band, and other ensembles for the musical.
courses.prerequisites: Intermediate Concert Band

courses.description: This course is for those who wish to learn to play the piano. We will work on basic theory, technique, and playing solo songs. No experience playing the piano is needed. Any skill level can join the class. Learn how to play your favorite song! This course may be taken more than once to continue to build upon your skills.

This class is for students regardless of previous instrument playing experience. Having a guitar is preferred but not required. Learn to read music, play chords, scales, and work on learning some of your favorite songs. We will work on strumming, picking, and finger-picking techniques. We will focus on hand position, music theory, and how to put chords together smoothly and in tempo.

This course is designed for students to be able to express themselves with music as well as learning music theory. The course will touch upon just some of the ways society creates music in our technological age. Students will learn how to make their own songs using only a computer. Using technology such as Garage Band, they will create their own musical pieces and learn about other ways music and technology go hand in hand. Students will explore digital musicianship while learning how songs are put together. At the same time, they will learn the basics of music theory, note names, rhythms, chord progressions, song form and more. Students will leave this course with their own original music.

Are you interested in the theatrical arts? Students can explore their true acting potential in this course. They will have an introduction to the theater as well as learn the basics of the stage. They will hear about the different types of shows and playwrights and get to know some acting techniques.

This class is a chance for kids who play guitar, bass, keyboards, or drums to play in a band with other motivated, like-minded young musicians. We go beyond simply learning the opening riffs to your favorite songs and instead learn ALL the parts of each song (intro, verses, choruses, bridge, solos, endings) in order to build a set list throughout the year that we will perform for a final end-of-the-year concert. Students will also learn how to put on their own show by tackling skills like lighting, sound, and stagecraft. We will tackle classic rock songs starting from the 1950s and progress up through more modern selections with opportunities for creating our own arrangements and compositions as well.
courses.prerequisites: Approval from the Rock Band teacher.

courses.description: This course is for somewhat advanced students who have participated in Middle School String Orchestra and have demonstrated advancing technical skills. Master musicianship, technique, and performance related music theory skills will be emphasized. Students will perform music commensurate with grade level II - III (on a music grading scale of I-VI). Some activities will occur outside of the regular class period. Concerts are required of all students in the orchestra program. Participation in District and All State music festivals will be encouraged.
courses.prerequisites: Previous MS String Orchestra experience

courses.description: Work-Based Learning allows students to earn high school credits and achieve academic proficiencies and to prepare for college and career by working with local industry or community professionals. Work experience must be directly related to a college or career path. Typical placements are apprenticeships, licensing programs, entry level career positions in advanced manufacturing or the trades, or internships for pre-college learning and development. A training plan and a WBL agreement are required, and must be completed and approved prior to enrollment in this program. Duration and
courses.credits_text: Credits and Duration determined on individual student and placement, not to exceed 3 credits
courses.prerequisites: Instructor’s permission and a Complete WBL Learning Plan on record.

courses.description: All grade nine through eleven students will be enrolled in NEST, a teacher-student advisory. NEST meets during T-Bird Time each Monday and additional days as needed. During NEST students will develop their Social and Emotional Learning Skills and work within their Personalized Learning Plans (PLP) to explore post high school opportunities, education, and training. Students will be graded on the MVSD SEL competencies.

Credit recovery is designed to keep students on schedule to graduate on time. In addition, credit recovery is designed as production oriented student directed learning. It provides another level of academic support to students by supplying students with available resources. Students celebrate success by actively participating in their learning.

Students will be recommended to Academic Core Support for targeted math and reading intervention MATH AND READING INTERVENTION During Academic Core Support, students in need of targeted math and/or reading skills remediation will receive instruction from our Math and/or Reading Interventionist, who will focus on the prerequisite skills necessary for success.

Missisquoi Valley Union High School students can enroll in a variety of high interest and flexibly paced virtual learning options through Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative and Edmentum. Students can supplement their in-person schedule by enrolling in offerings that are not available at MVU or they are unable to fit into their busy schedules. Students can reserve time in their schedule for virtual learning options or independently work on these courses outside of the school day. Students work with their school counselors to select virtual options and obtain required administrative approval.
courses.provider: Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative and Edmentum

courses.description: The Vermont State College System in conjunction with the State of Vermont, has created the Dual Enrollment Program which enables Vermont students to access two free college level courses during junior and/or senior years of high school. The tuition voucher can be used at any of the Vermont State Colleges, the University of Vermont, and other selected private colleges. The course is recorded as both high school credit and college credit, and credit may transfer to the college of choice following graduation. Students interested in taking any dual enrollment courses must first work with their school counselors to apply for the voucher.
courses.provider: Vermont colleges (CCV, Vermont State Colleges, UVM and other selected private colleges)

courses.description: With the 2013 passage of the Flexible Pathways bill (Act 77) and the establishment of Vermont’s Early College Program (ECP), access to Vermont State Colleges, the University of Vermont, and other postsecondary schools located in Vermont has been expanded. Colleges throughout the state offer an early admission program that allows high school seniors to take a full year of college level classes. The ECP simultaneously serves as a student’s senior year of high school and a full first year of college credit. For specific information regarding ECP opportunities, go to https://education.vermont.gov/student-learning/flexible-pathways/early-college.
courses.provider: Vermont State Colleges, University of Vermont and other Vermont postsecondary schools

courses.course_name: Vermont Academy of Science and Technology (VAST)
courses.description: Vermont Academy of Science and Technology (VAST) is a full-year Early College and High School completion program for High School Seniors. VAST is an independent, accredited high school exclusively for high school seniors. At VAST, students receive a high school diploma and complete a year of college at the same time through Vermont Technical College. Planning for this option must start at the beginning of junior year so that prerequisite steps can be completed before the application deadline. Further information is available online at https://www.vtc.edu/academics/vermont-academy-science-technology-vast.

courses.fulfills_text: The following classes at Northwest Career and Technical Center will qualify as an English Language Art credit upon completion of the second year of the following programs: Human Services I/II, Medical Professions I/II, and Cosmetology I/II. Must be in Senior standing and complete both years of the program for English credit during their senior year only.
courses.notes: Named only in the ELA credit options section; one of ten technical programs NCTC offers to grades 10-12 (others not named). Grade levels from the catalog letter (grades ten, eleven, twelve)

Must be in Senior standing and complete both years of the program for English credit during their senior year only.
courses.notes: Named only in the ELA credit options section; one of ten technical programs NCTC offers to grades 10-12 (others not named). Grade levels from the catalog letter (grades ten, eleven, twelve)

Must be in Senior standing and complete both years of the program for English credit during their senior year only.
